design_detail: Cochrane systematic review with meta-analysis (CD004332, version pub2, the first full review; protocol published 2003) of double-blind randomised controlled trials of acamprosate, alone or combined with naltrexone, against placebo or another medicine, in people with DSM or ICD alcohol dependence, with at least four weeks of treatment. RevMan 5 random-effects pooling of aggregate data from publications, manufacturer reports and investigators (Mantel-Haenszel risk ratios and risk differences, inverse-variance mean differences), plus a one-stage multilevel individual-patient-data (IPD) analysis of the two primary outcomes on a database to which the manufacturer gave access; end-of-treatment values, with post-treatment follow-up where available. Searches to January 2009. 24 trials (6894 participants by the results text; 6915 in the abstract) included; the main analysis of return to any drinking uses all 24 trials and 6172 participants.
can_establish: The average difference at the end of treatment, and 3 to 12 months later in a subset of trials, between acamprosate (as given in the trials, mostly 1332 or 1998 mg a day according to body weight, for 8 weeks to 12 months alongside psychosocial treatment) and placebo in the proportion of detoxified, mostly European outpatients with alcohol dependence who returned to any drinking, in the percentage of abstinent days, in return to heavy drinking, GGT and side effects, across the double-blind trials available to the reviewers by January 2009.
cannot_establish: Whether acamprosate reduces heavy drinking (null in the 6 trials that reported it) or helps people who are still drinking, have psychiatric comorbidity (excluded from most trials) or are treated without psychosocial support; how it compares with naltrexone or whether the combination adds benefit (2 or 3 trials); serious harms (not reported); why effects vary so much between trials (heterogeneity not investigated; I2 94% for abstinent days); and how far the result depends on industry-run trials and manufacturer-held data, beyond the funding comparison reported.

sample.recruitment: Search of CENTRAL (The Cochrane Library issue 2, 2009), MEDLINE (1966 to January 2009), EMBASE (1988 to January 2009) and CINAHL (1982 to January 2009) without language or other limits, four trial and results registers, contact with principal investigators of trials completed before 30 April 2009, key informants, experts, public sponsors and the manufacturer, Merck Serono (Geneva), and reference lists; the manufacturer gave access to an IPD database (Methods › Search methods for identification of studies; Selection of studies). The trials enrolled detoxified people with DSM-III, DSM-III-R, DSM-IV or ICD-10 alcohol dependence, as outpatients in all but one trial.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: double-blind RCTs with the individual as unit of randomisation, comparing acamprosate (any dose, alone or combined) with placebo or another medicine for alcohol dependence on drinking outcomes; at least four weeks of treatment; for post-treatment analyses at least 12 weeks of follow-up; crossover designs only with washout; mixed dependence and DSM abuse samples if dependence was the majority (over 50%). Excluded at full text (24 studies, listed with reasons): open-label designs (12), no placebo or active control (5), treatment shorter than 30 days (4), non-dependent sample (1), crossover without first-period data (1), single-blind design (1). Post-treatment results of Chick 2000 (4 weeks) and Mason 2006 (8 weeks) and the single-blind placebo phase of Paille 1995 were excluded.
sample.demographics: Adults aged 18 or over except one trial of adolescents (Niederhofer 2002, inpatients, mean age 17.1, 26 participants); otherwise mean age 40 to 47 (median 42). Mostly mixed-sex samples with men the majority; two trials enrolled men only. 19 trials in Europe, 2 in the USA (Anton 2006; Mason 2006) and one each in South Korea, Australia and Brazil; 18 multicentre; sample sizes 10 (Borg 2003) to 1383 (COMBINE, Anton 2006). Treatment lasted 8 weeks to one year, six months in 10 trials. Most trials excluded concurrent major psychiatric disorders.
sample.attrition: For binary outcomes the review analysed everyone randomised and counted drop-outs and people lost to follow-up as having relapsed; the aggregate abstinent-days data were taken as reported, while the IPD analysis counted all time after an early drop-out as non-abstinent. Drop-out in the trials was high, often 40 to 80% of an arm (for example 65.4% and 64.7% in Chick 2000; 52.7% and 79% in Pelc 1992), and was significantly higher on acamprosate in Mason 2006 (56.3% against 44.4%). Pooled drop-out for any reason: RR 0.91 (0.83 to 0.99), 22 trials, 6111 participants (Data and analyses, Comparison 1, outcome 16).
sample.selection_effects: Detoxified, treatment-seeking outpatients, mostly in Europe, mostly without psychiatric comorbidity, receiving psychosocial treatment that most publications did not specify. 17 of the 24 trials were sponsored and run by industry within new drug application processes (11) or received the manufacturer's grants and facilities (6). Several key outcomes came from manufacturer reports or the sponsor rather than publications (return to any drinking for 4 trials, abstinent days for 4, including the unpublished Borg 2003 with data on file at Lipha). Studies were selected by one author, with a second consulted only in case of uncertainty.

exposure.measurement: The randomised intervention: acamprosate, against placebo (all trials but the naltrexone comparisons), naltrexone (3 trials) or naltrexone plus acamprosate (2 trials). Adherence by pill count in most trials, with acamprosate plasma levels in one (Mason 2006). Drinking was self-reported by retrospective quantity-frequency reports or drinking cards in most trials and by Timeline Follow-Back in four; 17 trials checked self-reports with GGT, carbohydrate-deficient transferrin, mean corpuscular volume, breath or urine alcohol or collateral reports (Results › Included studies › Methods of data assessment).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as the review reports them: oral acamprosate dosed by body weight in most trials (1332 mg a day below 60 kg, 1998 mg above), 1332 mg a day in two trials, 3000 mg a day in the two US trials, and 1000 to 2250 mg by weight in Lhuintre 1985; three trials compared doses. Treatment lasted 8 weeks to one year. Most trials required 3 to 7 days of abstinence after detoxification before randomisation (12 and 14 days in two); Mason 2006 did not require detoxification and about half its sample was drinking; Gual 2001 started acamprosate at the beginning of withdrawal.
exposure.polysubstance: Most trials excluded concurrent drug use and psychotropic medication; some permitted benzodiazepines started long before the trial, low-dose antidepressants or neuroleptics, or voluntary disulfiram (Besson 1998, Poldrugo 1997).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable as a test condition: return to drinking and abstinent days are the outcomes.

comparison.controls: Placebo in all 24 trials (18 two-arm trials, three dose-comparison trials, Morley 2006 and the two four-arm trials); naltrexone in 3 trials (Anton 2006; Kiefer 2003; Morley 2006); naltrexone plus acamprosate in 2 (Anton 2006; Kiefer 2003). Psychosocial treatment accompanied both arms but was not specified in most publications; eight trials encouraged Alcoholics Anonymous attendance.
comparison.matching: Randomisation. Review's own judgments: sequence generation described (all adequate) in 6 of 24 trials; allocation concealment adequate in 3 (Kiefer 2003; Mason 2006; Morley 2006), high risk in one (Namkoong 2003, randomised by the principal investigator) and unclear in the rest; blinding adequate in 7, with integrity tested and confirmed in 2; baseline equivalence and equal medication adherence ('free of other bias') in 13, unclear in 11 (Results › Risk of bias in included studies; study tables).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to randomised comparisons; baseline equivalence and equal adherence were judged under other bias.

outcomes.instruments: Primary: return to any drinking (binary; the complement of continuous abstinence) and cumulative abstinence duration (percentage of study days abstinent). Secondary: return to heavy drinking (as each trial defined it), GGT (units per litre) and side effects. Drop-out and drop-out due to adverse events were analysed as moderators. Post-treatment analyses were limited to the primary outcomes. The primary outcomes were also estimated from IPD.
outcomes.validity_norms: Exposure units: heavy drinking was 5 or more standard drinks in most of the six trials reporting it, 6 in Morley 2006; Kiefer 2003 also counted drinking on 5 or more days a week, and Chick 2000 defined it as 5 (3) standard drinks a day for men (women) or a single day of 8 (6); where trials did not state the alcohol content of a standard drink, ICAP 2003 country values were used. The reference group is placebo (or the named active control). Side effects were ascertained by checklists, open enquiry, a rating scale, SAFTEE or spontaneous reports.
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit: fewer people returning to any drinking, more abstinent days. Harm: risk differences for side effects, of which only those with significant group differences were treated as clinically relevant; serious adverse events are not reported as an outcome. No minimal clinically important difference was defined.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 5 counts the review's outcome families for acamprosate against placebo (two primary, two secondary efficacy outcomes and side effects). The data table holds 45 top-level pooled analyses across five comparisons, plus side-effect subtotals (26 of them against placebo); each was tested at p of 0.05 or below.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Trial level, by the review's judgments: blinding of patients and research staff with an identical placebo adequate in 7 of 24 trials, tested and confirmed in 2; objective checks of self-reported drinking in 17. Review level: outcome statistics coded independently by two authors; risk of bias rated by one author and checked by a second; the IPD analysis was done by one author (Lehert).

analysis.effect_sizes: Acamprosate against placebo, end of treatment (random effects unless stated): return to any drinking RR 0.86 (95% CI 0.81 to 0.91), 24 trials, 6172 participants, tau-squared 0.01, NNTB 9.09 (6.66 to 14.28); abstinent days MD 10.94 percentage points (5.08 to 16.81), 19 trials, 5224, I2 94%, tau-squared 138.67; return to heavy drinking RR 0.99 (0.94 to 1.04), 6 trials, 2132, I2 0%, fixed-effect RR 0.97 (0.92 to 1.03); GGT MD -11.91 U/L (-24.12 to 0.30), 7 trials, 1650, I2 80%, tau-squared 197.21. Diarrhoea RD 0.11 (0.09 to 0.13), 16 trials, 4486 (fixed effect), NNTH 9.09 (7.69 to 11.11); no other side effect more frequent. Drop-out due to adverse events RR 1.35 (1.01 to 1.80), 19 trials, 5763; drop-out for any reason RR 0.91 (0.83 to 0.99), 22 trials, 6111. Post-treatment (3 to 12 months): return to any drinking RR 0.91 (0.87 to 0.96), 7 trials, 1986, NNTB 12.50 (9.09 to 25.00); abstinent days MD 8.92 (5.08 to 12.77), 9 trials, 3069. IPD (discussion only): return to any drinking RR 0.83 (0.79 to 0.87), NNTB 7.14 (5.15 to 11.76); abstinent days MD 9.82 (8.05 to 11.35). By funding: fully industry-sponsored RR 0.88 (0.80 to 0.97), 11 trials, 2858; partly industry-supported 0.84 (0.78 to 0.89), 6 trials, 1765; non-profit 0.88 (0.81 to 0.96), 7 trials, 1549. Acamprosate against naltrexone: any drinking RR 1.03 (0.96 to 1.10), 3 trials, 800; abstinent days MD 2.98 (-7.45 to 13.42), 2 trials, 720; heavy drinking RR 1.04 (0.95 to 1.15). Acamprosate plus naltrexone against placebo: any drinking RR 0.70 (0.35 to 1.39), 2 trials, 694; against acamprosate alone 0.80 (0.49 to 1.30), 2 trials, 688. Editors' calculations: the NNTBs correspond to risk differences of about 0.11 (0.07 to 0.15) at the end of treatment, 0.14 (0.09 to 0.19) in the IPD analysis and 0.08 (0.04 to 0.11) after treatment; approximate 95% prediction intervals from the printed tau-squared values (t distribution, k-2 degrees of freedom) are RR 0.69 to 1.07 for return to any drinking, -14.7 to 36.6 percentage points for abstinent days and -51.4 to 27.6 U/L for GGT; a test of the three funding subgroups gives Q of about 1.0 (2 df, p of about 0.61). No control-group event rates or absolute numbers per arm are printed outside the forest plots, which are images.
analysis.covariates: None at review level (randomised comparisons). The IPD model for abstinent days had random treatment effects and fixed study effects; covariates, if any, are not stated.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Cochrane protocol published in Issue 3, 2003 (with a substantive amendment listed for 23 January 2007); review first published Issue 9, 2010, amended on 9 March 2010, 23 November 2010 (minimal editorial corrections) and 21 December 2010 (correction of an error in Analysis 1.5). The differences between protocol and review list: three authors added (Hackl-Herrwerth, Vecchi, Lehert); return to heavy drinking, available from six trials, moved from the primary to the secondary outcomes and abstinent days (19 trials) promoted to primary after data extraction; drop-out moved from an efficacy outcome to a moderator; IPD analyses added because the data set was not available when the protocol was written; tau-squared and Egger's test added; the planned sensitivity analysis for within-study selective outcome reporting not done and a funding-source analysis done instead. The planned meta-regression was postponed (Methods › Subgroup analysis and investigation of heterogeneity).
analysis.selective_reporting: Return to heavy drinking, a primary outcome in the protocol and null in the review, was demoted after data extraction; the review still reports it. The IPD results, which the abstract says verified the primary outcomes, appear only in the discussion, without the number of patients, heterogeneity or model output. Serious adverse events are not reported. The diarrhoea analysis uses a fixed-effect model although the methods state random effects for pooled outcomes.
analysis.power: Not addressed. The primary any-drinking estimate rests on 24 trials (6172 participants); return to heavy drinking on 6 trials; GGT on 7; comparisons with naltrexone on 2 or 3 trials and some side effects and GGT comparisons on a single trial of 80.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 24 double-blind trials, mostly European and mostly run or supported by the manufacturer, acamprosate given after detoxification alongside psychosocial treatment reduced the proportion returning to any drinking (RR 0.86, 0.81 to 0.91; NNTB about 9) and increased abstinent days by about 11 percentage points (MD 10.94, 5.08 to 16.81, with I2 94% and an editors' approximate prediction interval of -14.7 to 36.6), with no effect on return to heavy drinking (RR 0.99, 0.94 to 1.04; 6 trials) and a non-significant reduction in GGT. Diarrhoea was more frequent (RD 0.11) and drop-out because of adverse events was higher (RR 1.35, 1.01 to 1.80), while drop-out for any reason was lower (RR 0.91, 0.83 to 0.99). The reduction in return to any drinking persisted 3 to 12 months after treatment in 7 trials (RR 0.91, 0.87 to 0.96). Direct comparisons with naltrexone and with the combination (2 or 3 trials) showed no significant differences.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that "Acamprosate appears to be an effective and safe treatment strategy for supporting continuous abstinence" after detoxification. Gaps: (1) the plain language summary and the discussion state that side effects did not lead more people to stop acamprosate, while the review's own analysis shows a significant increase (RR 1.35, 1.01 to 1.80; 19 trials), which the discussion cites in the same sentence; (2) the IPD analysis that the abstract says verified the primary outcomes was not in the protocol, is reported only in two sentences of the discussion, rests on a database part-funded by the manufacturer and was run by an author who declares Merck honoraria and co-authored several of the included trials; (3) return to heavy drinking was a primary outcome in the protocol, was demoted after data extraction and is null, and the discussion explains the null result by saying acamprosate is mainly indicated for abstinence, a rationale given after the result; (4) the quality-of-evidence section says the trial features ensure a high level of validity, while allocation concealment was adequate in 3 of 24 trials, sequence generation reported in 6 and blinding adequate in 7; (5) 'safe' rests on side-effect lists from trials of 8 weeks to one year, and no serious adverse events are reported; (6) the risk of unblinding is called low because acamprosate is well tolerated, although diarrhoea was 11 percentage points more frequent on it; (7) the abstract reports identical effects in industry and non-profit trials, while the results text gives a different non-profit estimate (0.86) and the largest effect was in trials with manufacturer grants (0.84), and COMBINE, whose medication the manufacturer donated, is classed as non-profit here but as industry-sponsored in the companion naltrexone review. Against this, the abstract reports the null heavy-drinking and GGT results, the effects are called moderate, and the authors state that they reflect add-on benefit over psychosocial treatment.

timeline.event: Lhuintre et al. (Lancet), the earliest included placebo-controlled trial of acamprosate (calcium acetyl homotaurinate).
Protocol of this Cochrane review published (Issue 3, 2003).

Mann, Lehert and Morgan, meta-analysis of 17 trials (4087 patients), cited here with NNTB 7.8 (6.0 to 12.2) at 6 months and 7.5 (5.3 to 12.8) at 12 months; Bouza et al., 11 trials (3324 patients), NNTB 10 (7.0 to 14.0).
COMBINE (Anton et al.), Mason et al. and Morley et al., the newer trials the authors name as negative and as the reason for this review's smaller effect; all included.

Rösner, Leucht, Lehert and Soyka, meta-analysis by four authors of this review (21 trials, 5280 patients), cited with RR 0.84 (0.78 to 0.91) for return to any drinking and NNTB 7.7 (5.6 to 13.0); its title contrasts acamprosate supporting abstinence with naltrexone preventing excessive drinking.

This review, the first Cochrane review of acamprosate; amended on 21 December 2010 to correct an error in Analysis 1.5 (diarrhoea). The companion Cochrane review of opioid antagonists by the same team (Rösner et al., 2010, CD001867.pub3; card sc_rosner_2010a) shares the three acamprosate-naltrexone trials and the two combination trials.
Maisel et al., meta-analysis of naltrexone and acamprosate asking when each is most helpful (alcohol list Tier B, item 68; not read for this card).

Jonas et al., systematic review and meta-analysis of pharmacotherapy for alcohol use disorders in outpatient settings (alcohol list Tier A, item 29; not read for this card); claims should check its overlap with this review.
McPheeters et al., update of Jonas et al. (alcohol list Tier A, item 30; not read for this card).

replication.where_it_stands: This review pooled the double-blind acamprosate trials available to January 2009 and supports a modest increase in continuous abstinence after detoxification, with no effect on heavy drinking, in mostly European trials run or supported by the manufacturer. Its estimates are not independent of the earlier meta-analyses it compares itself with (Mann 2004; Rösner 2008), which share authors and many trials, and its head-to-head and combination comparisons share their trials with the companion naltrexone review. The contrast often drawn between acamprosate for abstinence and naltrexone for heavy drinking rests on different outcome choices in the two reviews; in the three direct comparisons neither drug differed from the other on any drinking outcome. Later reviews on the alcohol list (Jonas et al., 2014; McPheeters et al., 2023) cover the same question; claims must not count shared trials as independent support. The version read carries the December 2010 amendment; whether the Cochrane Library holds a later version was not checked in this session.

funding.funder: Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF), Germany, grant 01KG0724 (financial support and salary); internal support from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and Technical University of Munich (infrastructure). The IPD database was built from 2005 in a project initiated by the Plinius Major Society, described as a private initiative of European alcoholism investigators, and funded by non-industry national grants and a grant from Merck Serono (Geneva), which gave the reviewers unconditioned access to it. The acknowledgements state that responsibility for the content remains with the authors.
funding.declared_conflicts: Rösner, Hackl-Herrwerth and Vecchi: no conflict of interest known. Leucht: speaker, consultancy or advisory board honoraria from Sanofi-Aventis, BMS, EliLilly, Janssen/Johnson and Johnson, Lundbeck and Pfizer. Lehert: speaker, consultancy or advisory board honoraria from Lundbeck, SanofiAventis, Merck (the printed list ends with a comma). Soyka: speaker, consultancy or advisory board honoraria from Lipha Pharmaceuticals, Forest Laboratories, Sanofi-Aventis, Essex Pharma, Eli Lilly, Prempharm and AstraZeneca.
funding.affiliations_note: By the study tables, 9 of the 24 trials were sponsored and organised by Lipha or Merck Lipha within new drug application processes (the other two fully industry-sponsored trials by MERAM and by Whan-In Pharmaceutical), 6 received Lipha or Merck Lipha grants and facilities, and Lipha donated medication to and monitored the sites of COMBINE, which the review classes as non-profit. Lehert, who ran the IPD analysis, is a co-author of five included trials (Besson 1998, Gual 2001, Mason 2006, Pelc 1992, Pelc 1997; a sixth, Ladewig 1993, lists a 'Leher P') and of several earlier pooled analyses cited here; Soyka is a co-author of the included trial Sass 1996. The only management of conflicts described is that at least one author without prior involvement in addiction treatment or research took part in each review step. These are flags for closer reading, not reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Large, registered, double-blind trials, independent of the manufacturer, in people with alcohol use disorder recruited from ordinary care (including people with psychiatric comorbidity and people not yet abstinent), comparing acamprosate with placebo and with naltrexone on prespecified abstinence and heavy-drinking outcomes, with principled handling of missing drinking data, biomarker-checked drinking, systematic recording of serious adverse events and at least 12 months of follow-up; and a fully reported IPD meta-analysis of all existing trials, with its data sources, heterogeneity and model output published, to explain the between-trial variation.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (DSM or ICD alcohol dependence), intervention (acamprosate alone or combined), comparators (placebo or other medicines) and outcomes are specified.

Cochrane protocol published in 2003; deviations are listed with reasons. The most consequential, justified by availability, was made after data extraction: return to heavy drinking, a protocol primary outcome that turned out null, was demoted and abstinent days promoted; the IPD analysis was also added after the protocol. A reader who weighs these more heavily may judge the item partly met; it does not change the overall rating.
Only double-blind randomised trials were eligible, without a stated reason for that choice.

Four databases with strategies in Appendix 2, no language or date limits, four trial and results registers, investigators, experts and the manufacturer contacted, reference lists searched, an unpublished trial included; search in January 2009, about 20 months before publication.
Eligibility was assessed by one author, with a second consulted only in case of uncertainty (Methods › Selection of studies).
Outcome statistics were coded by two authors in parallel and independently and compared value by value; study characteristics extracted by one author and checked by a second.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: 24 excluded full texts are listed with reasons (Characteristics of excluded studies).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Design, setting, country, diagnosis, required abstinence, baseline characteristics, doses, psychosocial treatment, outcomes, missing-data rates, funding and the source of each outcome (publication, manufacturer report or investigator) are tabulated for each trial.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Cochrane 2008 tool with stated criteria (sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete binary and continuous data, selective reporting, baseline equivalence and equal adherence), with support for each judgment; rated by one author and checked by a second. The card follows these judgments for the trials, which were not read.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: A financial-support row is given for every included trial, distinguishing industry-run, industry-supported and non-profit trials.

Random-effects pooling was used and justified by reference, but the item also requires investigation of the causes of heterogeneity, and the planned meta-regression was deferred although I2 was 94% for abstinent days and 80% for GGT. The diarrhoea analysis (corrected in December 2010) and one vomiting analysis use fixed-effect models without explanation, and the IPD analysis is described in the methods but its results, sample and heterogeneity are not reported in the results or the data tables. As in the companion naltrexone review, this is the decisive item: counting the random-effects pooling as sufficient would raise the rating to moderate.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: The only analysis by study characteristics is by funding source (labelled a risk-of-bias analysis); no analysis by the appraised domains (for example the 3 trials with adequate allocation concealment against the rest).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The quality-of-evidence section discusses poorly reported randomisation, blinding and concealment and notes that unclear concealment is associated with bias; met minimally, because the same section says the trial features ensure a high level of validity and the conclusions carry no caveat.

I2 and tau-squared are reported and heterogeneity is called high, but its sources were not investigated; the discussion attributes the non-significant GGT result to one outlier without showing an analysis.

Funnel plot and Egger's test for return to any drinking, discussed in the quality-of-evidence section. Weakly reported: the test counts 25 trials although 24 are pooled, and its unweighted standard error and the description of the funnel plot are identical to those of the companion naltrexone review (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding, the manufacturer's part in the IPD database and each author's declarations are reported; management is described only as including, in each step, an author without prior involvement in addiction research. The review does not address authors appraising trials they co-authored.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: One critical item is not met (11: the causes of large heterogeneity were not investigated, the planned meta-regression having been deferred, fixed-effect models were used for two side-effect analyses without explanation, and the IPD analysis is not reported in a checkable form), which under AMSTAR 2 gives low confidence; critical items 2, 4, 7, 9, 13 and 15 are met, 13 and 15 only minimally. Non-critical weaknesses: no reason given for restricting to double-blind trials (3), single-author study selection (5), no analysis of the impact of the appraised risk of bias (12) and heterogeneity not explained (14). The rating concerns how far the pooled numbers can be trusted as summaries; for the trials the card follows the review's own Cochrane appraisal (allocation concealment adequate in 3 of 24, sequence generation reported in 6, blinding adequate in 7). Beyond the instrument, readers should weigh that 17 of 24 trials were run or supported by the manufacturer, that several outcomes came from manufacturer reports, and that the IPD component was built with manufacturer funding and analysed by an author with declared Merck honoraria; the funding-subgroup analysis found no difference (p of about 0.61, editors' test). The review may be cited for the end-of-treatment and post-treatment estimates of acamprosate against placebo on return to any drinking and abstinent days, with their intervals, for the null result on return to heavy drinking, and for the diarrhoea and drop-out estimates; not for the IPD estimates as independent confirmation, not for safety beyond the side effects listed, and not for differences between acamprosate and naltrexone.

key_findings.finding: The search found 414 records (384 from databases, 30 from other sources); after 203 duplicates, 211 were screened, 48 full texts assessed and 24 excluded. 24 double-blind RCTs were included: 6894 patients by the results text (3563 given acamprosate, 2929 placebo, 402 naltrexone); the abstract, plain language summary, discussion and conclusions give 6915.
key_findings.locator: Results › Description of studies › Results of the search; Included studies, 1st paragraph; Abstract › Main results
key_findings.note: The two totals are not reconciled anywhere in the review.

key_findings.finding: Trial designs and funding: 18 trials compared acamprosate with placebo only; three compared doses with placebo (Mason 2006; Paille 1995; Pelc 1997); Morley 2006 added a naltrexone arm; Anton 2006 and Kiefer 2003 had four arms including naltrexone and the combination. 11 trials were sponsored, organised and conducted by industry within new drug application processes, 6 received the manufacturer's grants and facilities, and 7 were investigator-driven with non-profit funding. 19 trials were in Europe, 2 in the USA and one each in South Korea, Australia and Brazil.
key_findings.locator: Results › Description of studies › Included studies (Comparisons; Funding and design; Countries in which the studies were conducted)
key_findings.note: The text's funding lists name Pelc 1992 twice and Pelc 1997 not at all; the study tables show Pelc 1997 as industry-sponsored and Pelc 1992 as non-profit (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Return to any drinking, acamprosate against placebo at the end of treatment: RR 0.86 (95% CI 0.81 to 0.91), 24 trials, 6172 participants, random effects; NNTB 9.09 (6.66 to 14.28); tau-squared 0.01.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Comparison 1: Acamprosate versus placebo › Primary outcomes, 1st paragraph; Heterogeneity; Data and analyses, Comparison 1, outcome 1
key_findings.note: Editors' calculations: risk difference about 0.11 (0.07 to 0.15); approximate 95% prediction interval RR 0.69 to 1.07. The NNTB is the inverse of a risk difference rounded to two decimals, which is why the same figures, 9.09 (6.66 to 14.28), appear for return to heavy drinking in the companion naltrexone review. The discussion prints the lower limits as 0.80 and 6.55.

key_findings.finding: Cumulative abstinence duration (percentage of study days abstinent): MD 10.94 percentage points (5.08 to 16.81), 19 trials, 5224 participants, I2 94%, tau-squared 138.67; the authors translate this into about three more abstinent days a month.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Comparison 1 › Primary outcomes, 2nd paragraph; Heterogeneity; Data and analyses, Comparison 1, outcome 2; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' approximate 95% prediction interval: -14.7 to 36.6 percentage points. The results text prints the estimate as 10.9.

key_findings.finding: Secondary outcomes did not differ: return to heavy drinking RR 0.99 (0.94 to 1.04), 6 trials, 2132 participants, I2 0% (fixed effect 0.97, 0.92 to 1.03); GGT MD -11.91 U/L (-24.12 to 0.30), 7 trials, 1650, I2 80%, tau-squared 197.21.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Comparison 1 › Secondary outcomes; Sensitivity analyses; Heterogeneity; Data and analyses, Comparison 1, outcomes 3, 4 and 19

key_findings.finding: Diarrhoea was the only side effect more frequent on acamprosate: RD 0.11 (0.09 to 0.13), 16 trials, 4486 participants, fixed effect; NNTH 9.09 (7.69 to 11.11). Nausea (RD 0.02, -0.01 to 0.05; 5 trials), vomiting, abdominal pain, constipation, headache, pruritus and other listed side effects did not differ; vertigo, dry mouth and poor concentration were slightly less frequent on acamprosate in one or two trials. Serious adverse events are not reported.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Comparison 1 › Secondary outcomes (side effects paragraph); Data and analyses, Comparison 1, outcomes 5 to 14
key_findings.note: Analysis 1.5 was corrected on 21 December 2010 (What's new); the results text gives the lower limit as 0.10 and the abstract labels the diarrhoea figure NNTB.

key_findings.finding: Drop-out because of adverse events was more frequent on acamprosate: RR 1.35 (1.01 to 1.80), 19 trials, 5763 participants, described in the results as a significant difference. Drop-out for any reason was less frequent: RR 0.91 (0.83 to 0.99), 22 trials, 6111.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Comparison 1 (paragraphs on drop-out due to adverse events and drop-out for any cause); Data and analyses, Comparison 1, outcomes 15 and 16
key_findings.note: The plain language summary and the discussion say the opposite for drop-out due to adverse events (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: After treatment ended (3 to 12 months later): return to any drinking RR 0.91 (0.87 to 0.96), 7 trials, 1986 participants, NNTB 12.50 (9.09 to 25.00); abstinent days MD 8.92 (5.08 to 12.77), 9 trials, 3069.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Comparison 1 (post-treatment outcomes paragraph); Data and analyses, Comparison 1, outcomes 17 and 18
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: risk difference about 0.08 (0.04 to 0.11). The discussion says post-treatment data came from ten trials and the completeness section from eleven.

key_findings.finding: IPD analyses, reported only in the discussion: return to any drinking RR 0.83 (0.79 to 0.87), NNTB 7.14 (5.15 to 11.76); abstinent days MD 9.82 (8.05 to 11.35). The IPD analyses covered all trials except Niederhofer 2002 (26 patients).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Summary of main results, 1st paragraph; Overall completeness and applicability of evidence › Completeness of the database
key_findings.note: Not in the protocol; no number of patients, heterogeneity estimate or model output is given. By the editors' arithmetic the abstinent-days interval is centred on 9.70 rather than 9.82 and is about a quarter as wide as the aggregate interval despite I2 94% in the aggregate data; the review gives no information to check it.

key_findings.finding: By funding source, return to any drinking: fully industry-sponsored trials RR 0.88 (0.80 to 0.97), 11 trials, 2858 participants; trials with the manufacturer's grants and facilities 0.84 (0.78 to 0.89), 6 trials, 1765; non-profit trials 0.88 (0.81 to 0.96), 7 trials, 1549.
key_findings.locator: Data and analyses, Comparison 5, outcome 1; Results › Risk of bias in included studies › Other potential sources of bias › Founding sources; Abstract › Main results
key_findings.note: The results text gives the non-profit estimate as 0.86 (0.81 to 0.91), the overall pooled value; the table and abstract give 0.88 (0.81 to 0.96). Editors' test of the three subgroups: Q about 1.0, 2 df, p about 0.61.

key_findings.finding: Publication bias: the funnel plot for return to any drinking showed slight asymmetry with a gap at the bottom; Egger's test was not significant, unweighted (R2 0.23, p = 0.342, SE 1.440, n = 25) or weighted (R2 0.46, p = 0.861, SE 1.412, n = 25).
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies › Other potential sources of bias › Publication bias; Figure 4 legend
key_findings.note: n = 25 exceeds the 24 pooled trials; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias of the trials, review's judgments: sequence generation described (all adequate) in 6 of 24; allocation concealment adequate in 3 (Kiefer 2003; Mason 2006; Morley 2006); blinding adequate in 7, with integrity tested in 2; missing binary data handled adequately in 19 of 24, inadequately in 2 and unclearly in 3; missing abstinent-days data adequately in 13 of 19; no selective outcome reporting found; free of other bias in 13, unclear in 11.
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies › Allocation; Blinding; Incomplete outcome data; Selective reporting; Other potential sources of bias
key_findings.note: The study table for Namkoong 2003 rates allocation concealment at high risk (randomised by the principal investigator).

key_findings.finding: Acamprosate against naltrexone (Anton 2006; Kiefer 2003; Morley 2006): return to any drinking RR 1.03 (0.96 to 1.10), 3 trials, 800 participants; abstinent days MD 2.98 (-7.45 to 13.42), 2 trials, 720; return to heavy drinking RR 1.04 (0.95 to 1.15); GGT MD 9.7 (5.18 to 14.22) higher on acamprosate from one trial of 80 (Kiefer 2003). Diarrhoea was more frequent on acamprosate (RD 0.27, 0.21 to 0.33); nausea (-0.08, -0.13 to -0.03), somnolence (-0.07, -0.13 to -0.01), fatigue and vomiting on naltrexone. Drop-out due to adverse events RR 0.76 (0.37 to 1.58). Anton 2006 and Kiefer 2003 favoured naltrexone and Morley 2006 acamprosate on return to any drinking.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Comparison 2: Acamprosate versus naltrexone; Data and analyses, Comparison 2

key_findings.finding: Acamprosate plus naltrexone (Anton 2006; Kiefer 2003): against placebo, return to any drinking RR 0.70 (0.35 to 1.39) and to heavy drinking 0.71 (0.38 to 1.35), 2 trials, 694; more diarrhoea (RD 0.20), nausea (0.20), decreased appetite (0.11) and vomiting (0.09); drop-out due to adverse events RR 3.75 (1.33 to 10.55). Against acamprosate alone: return to any drinking 0.80 (0.49 to 1.30) and to heavy drinking 0.81 (0.50 to 1.34), 2 trials, 688; more nausea (0.18, 0.11 to 0.24) and vomiting (0.08); drop-out due to adverse events RR 1.41 (0.68 to 2.90).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Comparison 3: Acamprosate + naltrexone versus placebo; Comparison 4: Acamprosate + naltrexone versus acamprosate; Data and analyses, Comparisons 3 and 4

key_findings.finding: Study conditions: acamprosate was mostly dosed by body weight (1332 mg a day below 60 kg, 1998 mg above), at 1332 mg in two trials and 3000 mg in the two US trials; treatment lasted 8 weeks to one year (six months in 10 trials); most trials required 3 to 7 days of abstinence after detoxification; treatment was outpatient except for one trial of adolescent inpatients; psychosocial treatment was given but not specified in most publications.
key_findings.locator: Results › Description of studies › Included studies (Funding and design; Treatment regimen and duration); Discussion › Overall completeness and applicability of evidence › Applicability of the results

key_findings.finding: Outcome data from non-published sources: return to any drinking came from manufacturer reports for 3 trials (Lhuintre 1990; Mason 2006; Tempesta 2000), from the investigator for Anton 2006 and from the sponsor for the unpublished Borg 2003; abstinent days came from manufacturer reports for 3 trials (Barrias 1997; Ladewig 1993; Chick 2000) and from the sponsor for Borg 2003.
key_findings.locator: Results › Description of studies › Included studies (Outcomes); Characteristics of included studies, Notes rows

key_findings.finding: Earlier meta-analyses cited for comparison: Mann 2004 (17 trials, 4087 patients) NNTB 7.8 (6.0 to 12.2) at 6 months and 7.5 (5.3 to 12.8) at 12 months; Rösner 2008 (21 trials, 5280) RR 0.84 (0.78 to 0.91), NNTB 7.7 (5.6 to 13.0); Bouza 2004 (11 trials, 3324) NNTB 10 (7.0 to 14.0). The authors attribute their smaller effect to newer negative trials (Anton 2006; Mason 2006; Morley 2006).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Agreements and disagreements with other studies or reviews, 2nd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The plain language summary says side effects did not cause more participants to stop acamprosate, and the discussion says side effects did not more often lead to early termination, citing RR 1.35 (1.01 to 1.80); the results call this a statistically significant difference, and the interval excludes 1.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Plain language summary, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Summary of main results, 2nd paragraph; Results › Effects of interventions › Comparison 1 (drop-out due to adverse events); Data and analyses, Comparison 1, outcome 15
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims must use the analysis: drop-out because of adverse events was about a third higher on acamprosate (RR 1.35, 1.01 to 1.80), not unchanged.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of participants is 6894 in the results (3563 + 2929 + 402) and 6915 in the abstract, plain language summary, discussion and conclusions.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Description of studies › Included studies, 1st paragraph; Abstract › Main results
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite 24 trials with about 6900 participants, or the analysis-specific count (6172 for return to any drinking).

reporting_issues.issue: Funding classification: the text lists Pelc 1992 both among industry-run trials and among non-profit trials and omits Pelc 1997, whereas the study tables show Pelc 1997 as sponsored by Merck Lipha and Pelc 1992 as non-profit. COMBINE (Anton 2006), whose medication and placebo were donated and sites monitored by Lipha, is classed as non-profit here but as industry-sponsored in the companion naltrexone review by the same authors. The results text gives the non-profit estimate as 0.86 (0.81 to 0.91), identical to the overall pooled estimate, while the data table and abstract give 0.88 (0.81 to 0.96).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Description of studies › Included studies (Funding and design); Results › Risk of bias in included studies › Founding sources; Characteristics of included studies (Pelc 1992, Pelc 1997, Anton 2006); Data and analyses, Comparison 5
reporting_issues.consequence: The non-profit subgroup contains the largest trial, which had manufacturer involvement; the funding comparison should be cited from the data table and with this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: Egger's test is reported for n = 25 trials although 24 are pooled; its unweighted standard error (1.440) and the description of the funnel plot (slight asymmetry with a gap at the bottom) are identical to those reported in the companion naltrexone review for a different set of 29 trials; the funnel plot is cited together with Analysis 5.1, which is the funding analysis.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Risk of bias in included studies › Other potential sources of bias › Publication bias
reporting_issues.consequence: The publication-bias test cannot be checked from the review and should not be cited as clearing the pooled estimate of small-study effects.

reporting_issues.issue: The IPD analysis, which the abstract says verified the primary outcomes, is described in the methods but its results appear only in two sentences of the discussion, without the number of trials and patients analysed, heterogeneity or model output, and in no data table; its abstinent-days interval (8.05 to 11.35) is centred on 9.70 by the editors' arithmetic, not on the printed 9.82.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Data collection and analysis (IPD acquisition and management; Data synthesis); Discussion › Summary of main results, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The IPD estimates cannot be checked and rest on a manufacturer-supported database analysed by one author; they should not be cited as independent confirmation of the aggregate results.

reporting_issues.issue: The diarrhoea analysis (Analysis 1.5, corrected on 21 December 2010) uses a fixed-effect model although the methods specify random effects for pooled outcomes; the results text gives RD 0.11 (0.10 to 0.13) while the abstract and data table give 0.09 to 0.13; the abstract labels the number needed to harm as NNTB. The review does not say what the corrected error was.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, What's new; Data and analyses, Comparison 1, outcome 5; Results › Effects of interventions › Comparison 1 (side effects); Abstract › Main results
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the data-table value (0.11, 0.09 to 0.13) and note the fixed-effect model; the content of the December 2010 correction is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: Text slips in the side-effect comparisons: against naltrexone, fatigue is printed as RD -0.13 (-0.26 to -0.10), an interval not centred on the estimate (table: -0.26 to -0.01), and vomiting as -0.06 (-0.11 to 0.01) although listed as more frequent on naltrexone (table: -0.11 to -0.01); against acamprosate alone, the combination's GGT MD of +1.00 is described as lower; the text refers to 38 side effects while the data table lists 34 distinct ones (vertigo appears twice).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Effects of interventions › Comparisons 1, 2 and 4; Data and analyses, Comparisons 1, 2 and 4

reporting_issues.issue: Other inconsistencies: post-treatment data are said to come from 10 trials in the summary, 11 in the completeness section, and 7 and 9 trials in the results and data table; the return-to-any-drinking lower limit is 0.80 in the discussion and the NNTB lower limit 6.55 in the comparison with other reviews; the other-bias entries for Barrias 1997 and Besson 1998, both acamprosate-placebo trials, mention a naltrexone group.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion › Summary of main results; Completeness of the database; Agreements and disagreements with other studies or reviews; Characteristics of included studies (Barrias 1997, Besson 1998)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite the results and data-table values.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC12147086 (Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2010, Issue 9, CD004332, version pub2, dated 7 September 2010 on the page, copyright 2011; its DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD004332.pub2 matches the assigned DOI; the What's new table lists amendments of 9 March, 23 November and 21 December 2010, the last correcting an error in Analysis 1.5, so the page holds the amended version; no separate correction notice is linked): abstract, plain language summary, all sections, the Data and analyses summary tables (rendered as text), the characteristics of included, excluded and ongoing studies with the trial-level risk-of-bias tables, Appendices 1 and 2, what's new, history, acknowledgements, differences between protocol and review, contributions of authors, sources of support, declarations of interest and the reference list. The flow chart, the risk-of-bias graph and summary, the funnel plot and all forest plots are images and their values were not extracted. No supplementary files. The included trials were not read.
